blocks.text: Say you run a home fragrance brand and you send a creator your bestselling candle. They unbox it, light it, film the flame for ten seconds, and say it smells amazing. That clip gets a few hundred views and nobody buys. The problem isn't the creator. It's the brief.
What makes creator marketing for candle and home fragrance brands different

Creator marketing for candle and home fragrance brands has to sell a smell nobody watching can actually smell, so it has to sell the room, the mood and the moment the candle sits inside instead. A flame looks the same whether the wax is vanilla or cedar. What changes is what the creator is doing when it's lit: closing their laptop at the end of a work day, setting a table before guests arrive, reading in a bath. That context is the only thing a viewer can judge, so it has to carry the whole pitch.

This is why candle content that performs tends to look less like a product review and more like a short scene. The product is present but not the subject. The subject is the ritual around it, and the candle is what makes that ritual feel finished.

Creators who already post about their homes, their mornings or their evenings will do better with a candle brief than beauty or fashion creators borrowed from another category. Look at their feed before you reach out. If they already film slow mornings, styled shelves, dinner parties or quiet nights in, a candle slots straight into content they're already making. If their feed is fast cuts and trend audio, a candle will feel like an interruption.

It also helps to check what room their content is usually set in. A creator who films in a small, cluttered bedroom will struggle to make a candle look aspirational no matter how good the copy is. [How to evaluate a creator before working with them](/blog/how-to-evaluate-a-creator-before-working-with-them) covers how to check this kind of fit before you commit product or budget to someone.
What should you brief creators to film?
Give the creator a moment to recreate, not a list of shots. Instead of asking for

an unboxing and a lit candle shot," ask for a specific scene: lighting it while running a bath, lighting it the second they walk in from work, lighting it before a friend comes over for wine. Name the scent note and the feeling it's meant to create, and let the creator decide how that looks in their own home.

Scent notes translate into visual cues better than most categories realise. Warm, woody notes pair with blankets, low lamps and evenings. Fresh, citrus notes pair with mornings, open windows and tidy kitchens. Tell the creator which bucket the scent sits in and they'll find the right light and props without you scripting it line by line. [A creator brief template for ecommerce](/blog/creator-brief-template-for-ecommerce) is a useful starting structure if you've never written one.
Gifted or paid for candle creators?

Gifted product works well for candles because the unit cost is low enough to send widely, and a creator who genuinely likes the scent will often reshoot the ritual scene without being asked. Reserve paid fees or affiliate terms for creators whose past content shows they can produce the kind of styled, slow footage this category needs, since that's a harder skill than a quick demo. [Gifted vs paid creator collaborations](/blog/gifted-vs-paid-creator-collaborations) walks through how to decide which to offer and when to mix the two.

Repeat the creators who get the ritual right rather than chasing a new face for every candle in the range. A creator who understands your brand's version of a cosy evening will keep nailing it scent after scent, and that consistency is worth more than reach on a single post.
How do you know it's working?

Watch for comments asking what the candle smells like, where it's from, or where to buy the exact table lamp or blanket in shot. Those comments mean the scene did its job and made someone want to be in it. Track which creators' links or codes convert, not just which videos get views, since a dreamy clip with no clear next step won't move anyone to buy. Linkable's reporting shows tracked sales per creator alongside the content and reach, so you can see which rituals actually turn into orders rather than guessing from likes.
If a creator's content gets comments but no sales, check the caption and link placement before dropping them. Often the scene is right and the path to purchase is missing.

Pick two or three creators this week whose feeds already show the kind of room and routine your scent fits, and brief them on one specific moment rather than the product itself. If you're setting this up for the first time, [How to launch your first creator campaign on Linkable](/blog/launch-campaign-linkable) covers the setup end to end.

faqs.a: A brief description helps, but the scene does the real selling. Let the creator describe the scent in their own words once, then spend the rest of the clip showing the moment it fits into.
faqs.q: Should candle brands ask creators to describe the scent in words?

faqs.a: They rarely convert on their own because an unboxing only shows packaging, not the thing a buyer actually cares about. Pair any unboxing with a second clip showing the candle lit in use.
faqs.q: Do unboxing videos work for candle brands?

faqs.a: Send one or two scents tied to a clear moment rather than a full range. A creator asked to cover five scents in one video will rush all of them and nail none.
faqs.q: How many candles should you send a creator at once?

faqs.a: Platforms matter less than whether the creator's existing content is set in real homes rather than studios. [TikTok vs Instagram creators for ecommerce](/blog/tiktok-vs-instagram-creators-ecommerce) breaks down the platform differences if you're deciding where to focus.
